lead: A washing machine, a fitness band and a highway toll tag each hold a small computer that runs one program for years. That computer is an embedded system: built into the product, hidden from the user, sized to the job. Two families do this work. A microcontroller is one chip holding a CPU core, memory, timers and pins; it starts in microseconds and sips power. A single-board computer is a small PC with an operating system, RAM and networking. Choosing the wrong family is the most common hardware mistake in an IoT project.
prereq: You need: the control unit block from 2.4 and the sensor signal chain from 2.1.

blocks.text: An embedded system is a computer whose program is fixed at design time and whose purpose is to serve the product around it. A laptop is general purpose: you install new software on it. An embedded board ships with one firmware image and runs it until the product is thrown away. Five properties separate the two families from a PC.

items: Fixed function: one program, no user installing apps, no keyboard or screen.
Real-time response: an input must be answered inside a deadline. Real-time means the worst case is known in advance, not that the average is fast.
Small memory: kilobytes, not gigabytes, so the program must fit by design.
Low power: a battery node in a field may have to run for years.
Long life in harsh conditions: the board may sit in a street cabinet for ten years, in heat and dust.

blocks.text: A missed deadline is a failure even if every other answer was quick. That is why the software level matters as much as the chip.

Every microcontroller repeats the same block diagram. The CPU core fetches and executes instructions. Flash holds the program and keeps it when power is removed. SRAM holds variables and loses them at power-off. EEPROM keeps a few settings across a battery change. Timers count clock ticks and produce exact delays and PWM waveforms for actuators. The interrupt controller lets a pin or a timer stop the main program and run a short handler at once. GPIO pins are the general-purpose digital inputs and outputs. The ADC turns a voltage into a number. Serial buses — UART, I²C, SPI — talk to sensors and radio modules.

Two memory layouts exist. In a von Neumann machine one memory holds both program and data, so one bus carries both. In a Harvard machine they sit in separate memories with separate buses, so an instruction fetch and a data read happen in the same cycle. Most microcontrollers are Harvard and most PCs are von Neumann. Harvard gives fixed, predictable instruction timing, which control code needs.

The width — 8, 16 or 32 bit — is the size of the arithmetic registers. A wider core handles bigger numbers in one instruction. Clock speed is not throughput: a 16 MHz core averaging one instruction per four cycles runs about 4 million instructions per second, while a 1.5 GHz core does far more but with cache jitter.

items: Microprocessor: the CPU alone, needing external RAM, flash, clock and support chips.
Microcontroller (MCU): CPU, flash, SRAM, timers, ADC, serial buses and GPIO on one chip, running without an operating system.
System on chip (SoC): a die that adds radio, GPU or DSP blocks to a CPU, often running Linux.
Single-board computer (SBC): an SoC with RAM, storage, USB, video and a pin header on one board, running Linux.

blocks.text: Arduino Uno. The board carries an ATmega328P: an 8-bit core at 16 MHz, 32 KB flash, 2 KB SRAM, 1 KB EEPROM, 14 digital I/O pins, 6 analog inputs behind a 10-bit ADC, and 5 V logic. It has no operating system; the sketch starts within milliseconds of power-on.

Raspberry Pi 4. A Broadcom SoC with a 64-bit ARM Cortex-A72 quad core, 1 to 8 GB of RAM, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Ethernet, USB and HDMI, booting Linux from a microSD card in tens of seconds. Its 40-pin header works at 3.3 V and has no analog input at all.
ESP8266 and ESP32 sit in between: microcontrollers with a Wi-Fi radio on the same chip. The ESP32 adds a second core and Bluetooth Low Energy, and still runs no operating system unless you load one.

Three software levels fix the response time. Bare metal is one loop plus interrupt handlers, with response in microseconds and no scheduler. An RTOS adds tasks, priorities and a bounded context switch, with response in tens of microseconds. Linux gives files, processes and a network stack, but a GPIO edge reaches your program in milliseconds because the kernel schedules other work first. Choose the software level before the board.

items: List every input and output with its deadline. A motor current loop at 10 kHz needs a microcontroller; a temperature upload every minute does not.
Add up flash and SRAM for firmware and buffers. If it fits in tens of kilobytes, an MCU is enough.
Check the analog inputs. The Pi has none, so an external ADC over I²C is needed.
Check voltage. Arduino is 5 V logic and Pi GPIO is 3.3 V, so a 5 V sensor output needs a level shifter or a divider before it touches a Pi pin.
Check power. A node that must last a year on a cell wants an MCU that sleeps at microamps, not a Linux board drawing hundreds of milliamps.
Take the SBC only for a camera, a database, TLS-secured Wi-Fi, or Python libraries you cannot do without.

blocks.text: One line to remember: MCU for control, SBC for thinking. If you need both, run the fast loop on an MCU and let it talk over UART to the SBC.

examples.question: An Arduino Uno uses a 10-bit ADC with V_ref = 5.00 V. Find the resolution in mV, the code produced by an input of 1.20 V, and the input voltage that produces code 512.
steps: A 10-bit ADC divides the reference range into 2¹⁰ = 1024 steps, giving output codes 0 to 1023.
Resolution (one LSB) = V_ref / 2ⁿ = 5.00 V / 1024 = 0.0048828 V = 4.88 mV per step.
Code for 1.20 V = 1.20 V / 0.0048828 V = 245.76; the converter truncates, so the code is 245.
Check: 245 × 4.88 mV = 1196 mV, close to 1.20 V (the missing 4 mV is less than one step).
Check: 512/1024 = 0.5, and half of 5.00 V is 2.50 V.
examples.answer: Resolution = 4.88 mV per step, an input of 1.20 V gives code 245, and code 512 corresponds to 2.50 V.
examples.check:
vref = 5.00
bits = 10
levels = 2 ** bits
lsb_mV = vref / levels * 1000
print(round(lsb_mV, 2))
code = int(1.20 / (lsb_mV / 1000))
print(code)
vin2_mV = 512 * lsb_mV
print(round(vin2_mV, 1))
print(round(vin2_mV / 1000, 2))

examples.question: A 12-bit ADC has V_ref = 3.30 V. Find the resolution in mV and the code for an input of 1.00 V.
steps: Resolution = 3.30 V / 4096 = 0.0008057 V = 0.806 mV per step.
examples.answer: Resolution = 0.806 mV per step and 1.00 V gives code 1241.

traps: Raspberry Pi GPIO has no analog input. A sensor giving 0-5 V needs an external ADC, usually over I²C; connecting it straight to a pin does nothing useful.
Arduino drives 5 V logic and Pi GPIO is 3.3 V, and Pi pins are not 5 V tolerant. A divider or level shifter is mandatory, not optional.
Resolution is not accuracy. The 10-bit ADC gives 4.88 mV steps, but reference drift and sensor error can be tens of millivolts.
Clock speed is not instruction rate. 16 MHz does not mean 16 million instructions per second; the average is set by cycles per instruction.
On the Uno, variables live in 2 KB SRAM, not the 32 KB flash. Three float arrays of 200 elements need about 2400 bytes of RAM and overflow silently.

quiz.q: Define an embedded system and state three properties that separate it from a PC.
quiz.a: A computer built into a product to run one fixed program. Properties: fixed function, bounded (real-time) response, small memory, low power, long life.

quiz.q: List the ATmega328P figures quoted for the Arduino Uno.
quiz.a: 16 MHz 8-bit core, 32 KB flash, 2 KB SRAM, 1 KB EEPROM, 14 digital I/O, 6 analog inputs, 10-bit ADC, 5 V logic.

quiz.q: Why does a Harvard memory layout suit a control loop?
quiz.a: Program and data are in separate memories with separate buses, so a fetch and a data read occur in the same cycle. Instruction timing is fixed and predictable, which is what a deadline needs.

quiz.q: Why does a Raspberry Pi respond to a GPIO edge in milliseconds while an MCU responds in microseconds?
quiz.a: The MCU runs one program and jumps straight to the interrupt handler. On Linux the CPU is shared among processes, so the waiting program runs only when the kernel schedules it, adding millisecond jitter.

quiz.q: A 12-bit ADC has V_ref = 3.30 V. Find the resolution in mV and the code for 1.00 V.
A greenhouse node must sample soil moisture every 10 minutes and upload over Wi-Fi, and must cut a pump within 5 ms of a dry-run signal. Choose hardware and software and justify.
quiz.a: One ESP32 running bare metal or an RTOS: it has on-chip Wi-Fi for the upload and interrupt latency in microseconds, so the 5 ms cut is safe. The 10-minute task is trivial. A Raspberry Pi is a poor choice: Linux scheduling jitter can exceed 5 ms, and it would need an external ADC for the analog probe.

quiz.q: An Uno sketch declares three float arrays of 200 elements each. What happens, and why?
quiz.a: Each float is 4 bytes, so 200 elements take 800 bytes and three arrays need 2400 bytes, more than the 2048 bytes of SRAM. The program compiles and then corrupts memory at run time; the fix is fewer samples, smaller types, or external memory.

beyond: Not for the exam. Open-source RISC-V microcontroller cores are now competing with ARM Cortex-M in low-power designs, and the ESP32 family keeps adding radios (Thread, Zigbee, Matter) on the same die. Real-time operating systems such as Zephyr and FreeRTOS are the usual answer when a bare-metal loop outgrows itself. TinyML pushes small neural networks onto microcontrollers with tens of kilobytes of RAM. Industrial control still separates safety-rated PLCs from the microcontrollers that do the fast work. Search for RISC-V microcontrollers, Zephyr device trees, and TinyML benchmark figures if you want to go further.
